title: What the Ice Remembers and What It Loses
topic: ice cores as a record of past atmospheres
paragraphs: A drill working down through an ice sheet returns cylinders of ice about ten centimeters across, cut into meter lengths and boxed for the trip to a freezer laboratory.
What arrives looks like plumbing stock.
What it holds is an archive.

Every cylinder holds snow that fell on a particular set of days, the dust and salt and ash that fell with it, and, sealed inside small bubbles, a sample of the air the planet was breathing some time after that snow landed.
That last clause carries the first complication: the ice and the air trapped inside it are not the same age.
Turning snow into ice is slow mechanical work.
Fresh polar snow arrives with a density near one tenth that of water, most of its volume empty space between delicate crystals.
Under the weight of each new season those crystals round off, press together, and weld at their contact points, a process called sintering.
The intermediate material, denser than snow and not yet ice, is firn.
Firn is granular, porous, and connected: its pore space forms continuous channels that run all the way to the surface.
Solid glacial ice has a density of about 0.917 grams per cubic centimeter.
Because those channels stay open, the upper firn breathes.
Air from above moves down through it and back up, driven by pressure changes at the surface and by molecular diffusion, so the gas in open pores thirty meters down is very nearly modern.
How far that exchange reaches depends on temperature and snowfall.
On the cold, dry interior of East Antarctica the firn column can run past a hundred meters.
On a warm coastal dome with heavy accumulation it may be only fifty.
At the base of the column sits a lock in zone, a stack of layers dense enough that vertical mixing effectively stops.
Below the lock in zone, at a density near 0.83 grams per cubic centimeter, the remaining pores pinch shut and the air in them becomes a set of isolated bubbles.
That moment of closure, not the moment the snow fell, is the birthday of the gas sample.
The ice around a bubble has sat there as long as it took the firn column to bury it, so the air is always younger than the ice holding it.
The size of that age offset varies enormously, from a few decades at a wet coastal site to several thousand years at the coldest, driest inland sites during a glacial period.
The offset is not a nuisance to be waved away.
It is the central obstacle to the question the cores are most often asked.
Anyone asking whether carbon dioxide rose before or after a temperature change is comparing a measurement made on the gas with one made on the ice, and the two sit on different clocks.
Correcting for the difference requires a model of how the firn column behaved in the past, which itself requires estimates of past temperature and snowfall.
The uncertainty in that correction is often larger than the lead or the lag under debate.
Closure also blurs.

Air in the open firn is stirred over years to centuries before it is sealed, and bubbles do not all close at the same depth, so a laboratory measures a weighted average across a window of time rather than a snapshot of one year.
A sharp spike lasting a decade is flattened into a gentle rise, or lost.
The same mixing has a use, since methane spreads between the hemispheres within a couple of years and its swings can be matched from core to core.
The ice itself carries a second archive that owes nothing to bubbles.
Windblown mineral dust records the dryness and circulation of distant continents.
Sea salt tracks storms and sea ice.
Sulfate spikes mark explosive eruptions, ammonium marks biomass burning, and beryllium-10, produced when cosmic rays strike the upper atmosphere, tracks the magnetic activity of the sun.
Not everything survives equally well.

Greenland ice carries enough calcium carbonate dust to react with acids already in the ice and manufacture carbon dioxide inside the core itself, which is why Antarctic ice is the reference archive for past carbon dioxide.
The best known measurement made on the ice rather than the gas is the isotope ratio of the water molecules.
Most water is built from the lighter atoms, oxygen-16 and ordinary hydrogen, but a small fraction carries oxygen-18 or deuterium, the heavier form of hydrogen.
Heavy molecules evaporate slightly less readily and condense slightly more readily.
As an air mass travels from a warm ocean toward a cold pole it snows away its moisture, and each round of condensation removes heavy molecules first, leaving the vapor lighter.
The colder the final condensation, the more of that stripping has happened, and the lighter the snow that falls.
The chain of reasoning turns a chemical ratio into a thermometer.
The calibration in common use is a spatial one.
Measure the isotope ratio of recent snow at many sites across an ice sheet, plot each value against that site's modern mean annual temperature, and take the slope of the resulting line.
Applying that slope downward through a core converts an isotope profile into a temperature history.
The step from a line across space to a line through time is where care is required, and it is worth being blunt about what the reading assumes.
It assumes that snow fell in the same season then as now, that it came from the same ocean regions at the same sea surface temperatures, and that the ice surface stood at the same elevation.
None of these holds exactly.
If a colder climate suppresses winter snowfall, the surviving layers are weighted toward summer and the record reads warm.
If the ice sheet stood taller, its surface was colder for reasons unrelated to the climate at sea level.
The thermometer is not wrong, but it is conditional, and reading it as a direct account of air temperature claims more than it can deliver.
What rescues it is that the ice offers thermometers of other kinds.
An ice sheet conducts heat poorly, so a borehole holds a faint temperature profile left by past surface conditions, which can be inverted for a coarse history.

During an abrupt warming, the sudden temperature contrast across the firn column sorts nitrogen and argon isotopes by mass, leaving a fingerprint in the trapped gas that records the size of the temperature jump directly.
Applied to Greenland, these methods indicated a change from the last glacial period to the present close to twice what the spatial slope alone suggested.
Dating begins with counting.
Near the top of a core the layers are visible, bands of coarse summer crystals alternating with fine winter ones.
Deeper down, chemistry keeps the calendar.
Dust and sodium peak in one season, hydrogen peroxide and the water isotopes in another, and a probe drawn along the core measures electrical conductivity, which traces acidity layer by layer.
Counting works where snowfall is heavy.
Central Greenland receives roughly twenty centimeters of ice equivalent accumulation a year, enough that single years stay thick enough to resolve well back into the last glacial period.
Error accumulates as the count runs, from a year or two per thousand in recent millennia to hundreds by forty thousand.
Counting alone would drift, so the count is pinned.

A large explosive eruption injects sulfate into the stratosphere and deposits it in both hemispheres within a couple of years, leaving one horizon that shows up in Greenland and Antarctic cores alike.
Eruptions with known historical dates anchor the recent count outright.
Farther back, sharp beryllium-10 peaks produced by extreme solar events appear in the ice and in the radiocarbon of tree rings at the same moment, tying two independent chronologies together.
The deepest ice is the least trustworthy, and the reasons compound.
An ice sheet spreads under its own weight, so every annual layer is stretched sideways and thinned as it is buried.
A layer twenty centimeters thick at the surface may be a centimeter thick halfway down and a fraction of a millimeter near the bed.
Once layers are that thin, diffusion of water molecules through the solid smears the isotope cycles until annual structure is gone.
Geothermal heat can melt the bottom away, removing the oldest ice.
Worse, ice near bedrock flows around obstacles and can fold back over itself, stacking older ice above younger.
Two deep Greenland cores drilled near one another agreed for most of their length and disagreed in the bottom tenth, which is how that disturbance was found.
Below the depth where counting fails, chronology comes from models of ice flow and from matching features in the record to the known rhythm of the orbital cycles of Earth.
This is a reasonable procedure and a weaker one, and the resulting ages carry uncertainties of thousands of years.

It is why the long Antarctic records, which reach back eight hundred thousand years, are used for what they are good at, the size and ordering of slow glacial cycles, rather than for the fine timing of a single event.
All of this shapes what the record can say about rates.
Smoothing in the firn and thinning at depth push the same way: both hide fast changes and preserve slow ones.
A hundred year excursion inside old, low accumulation ice would leave little trace.

The record therefore sets a floor under past rates of change rather than a ceiling, and a claim that nothing in the past matched the speed of the present rise is only as strong as the resolution of the ice behind it.
That claim holds up because it does not rest on the deep cores.
Sites with heavy snowfall resolve the last two thousand years to a decade or better, and across that stretch the record is flat.
None of this makes the archive less valuable.
Its limits are unusually well characterized.
The age offset can be modeled, the smoothing estimated, the thinning calculated, and the disturbed sections identified and set aside.
An archive whose distortions are known and bounded is worth far more than one that merely looks clean.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the air held inside a bubble in an ice core dates from
choices: the season in which the snow now surrounding it first fell
the moment the pores in the firn pinched shut and sealed it off
the year the core was drilled and lifted to the surface
the time when the firn column at that site first began to form
the point at which the ice reached a density of 0.917 grams per cubic centimeter

proof.quote: That moment of closure, not the moment the snow fell, is the birthday of the gas sample.
the remaining pores pinch shut and the air in them becomes a set of isolated bubbles

questions.why: Paragraph 4 says the moment of closure, not the moment the snow fell, is the birthday of the gas sample. Below the lock in zone the pores pinch shut and the air becomes isolated bubbles.
distractorNotes: The passage states the opposite, that the snow and the gas carry different dates and the gas is the younger of the two.
Drilling only recovers the sample. The passage dates the gas to closure in the firn, far below the modern surface.
The firn column at a site is far older than any single bubble in it, and paragraph 4 ties the gas age to pore closure.
The number 0.917 is the density of solid glacial ice given in paragraph 2, not the close off density of about 0.83 named in paragraph 4.

questions.stem: The passage says that acidity is traced layer by layer in a core by measuring
choices: the density of each band of crystals in the ice
the concentration of sea salt held in the ice
the ratio of oxygen-18 to ordinary oxygen-16
the amount of windblown mineral dust deposited in each layer
electrical conductivity along the core

proof.quote: measures electrical conductivity, which traces acidity layer by layer

questions.why: Paragraph 12 lists the seasonal markers and then says a probe drawn along the core measures electrical conductivity, which traces acidity layer by layer.
distractorNotes: Density tells you how far snow has turned into ice, which paragraph 2 covers, not how acidic a layer is.
Sea salt appears in paragraph 7 as a tracer of storms and sea ice, not as the acidity measurement.
The isotope ratio is the temperature proxy and one of the seasonal markers, not the way acidity is read.
Dust is named as a seasonal marker and as a continental tracer, but the acidity reading is the conductivity probe.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Antarctic ice rather than Greenland ice serves as the reference record for past carbon dioxide because
choices: Greenland cores rarely reach back far enough to cover a full glacial cycle of the kind Antarctic ice records
the firn column in Greenland is too shallow to seal any gas at all
carbonate dust in Greenland ice reacts with acids in the ice and makes carbon dioxide inside the core
Greenland receives too little snowfall for its annual layers to be counted
carbon dioxide mixes between the hemispheres far too slowly to ever reach Greenland

proof.quote: react with acids already in the ice and manufacture carbon dioxide inside the core itself

questions.why: Paragraph 7 says Greenland ice carries enough calcium carbonate dust to react with acids already in the ice and manufacture carbon dioxide inside the core itself.
distractorNotes: The passage never compares the two regions on length of record. The objection it raises is chemical contamination inside the core.
Greenland firn seals gas normally. Paragraph 7 objects to a reaction in the ice, not to a failure to trap bubbles.
Paragraph 12 says the opposite, that central Greenland's snowfall is heavy enough to make layer counting work well.
Paragraph 6 says methane crosses between the hemispheres in a couple of years, so slow mixing is not the problem raised here.

questions.stem: The passage presents the sorting of nitrogen and argon isotopes in the firn as a way to
choices: measure the size of an abrupt temperature jump directly
date the gas trapped at the bottom of the firn column
identify which season a given layer of snow fell in
detect the sulfate that a distant volcanic eruption left behind in the ice
estimate how much snow fell at a site during a glacial period

proof.quote: records the size of the temperature jump directly

questions.why: Paragraph 11 says that during an abrupt warming the temperature contrast across the firn sorts nitrogen and argon by mass, leaving a fingerprint in the trapped gas that records the size of the jump directly.
distractorNotes: The sorting records a temperature change, not an age. Dating comes from counting and flow models in paragraphs 12 through 15.
Seasonal identification comes from dust, sodium, hydrogen peroxide and the water isotopes in paragraph 12.
Volcanic sulfate is a dating tie point in paragraph 13 and has nothing to do with gas isotope sorting.
Snowfall estimates feed the firn model in paragraph 5. The isotope sorting described here reports a temperature change.

questions.stem: The passage says that sharp peaks of beryllium-10 are useful for dating because they
choices: appear only in ice that has never been disturbed by flow
mark the season in which each annual layer was deposited
record the total amount of sulfate a large eruption released
show up in the ice and in the radiocarbon of tree rings at the same moment
accumulate in the ice at a steady rate that can be converted directly into an age

proof.quote: appear in the ice and in the radiocarbon of tree rings at the same moment

questions.why: Paragraph 13 says beryllium-10 peaks from extreme solar events appear in the ice and in tree ring radiocarbon at the same moment, tying two independent chronologies together.
distractorNotes: The passage never links beryllium-10 to undisturbed ice. Its value is that it shows up in two separate archives at once.
Seasonal marking is done by dust, sodium, hydrogen peroxide and the water isotopes, as paragraph 12 explains.
Sulfate is the volcanic marker described just before this. Beryllium-10 comes from cosmic rays and solar events.
This describes a steady radiometric clock. The passage values beryllium-10 for matching two chronologies, not for decaying predictably.

questions.stem: As used in paragraph 3, "breathes" most nearly means that the upper firn
choices: expands and contracts as the temperature at the surface rises and falls
releases the gases that were sealed into it during earlier seasons of snowfall
exchanges air with the atmosphere through its connected pore spaces
supports living communities of microbes within its open pores
loses mass steadily to evaporation from the surface of the snow

proof.quote: Air from above moves down through it and back up
its pore space forms continuous channels that run all the way to the surface

questions.why: Paragraph 3 explains the word right after using it: air moves down and back up through the open channels, so the gas thirty meters down is very nearly modern.
distractorNotes: The word here is about air moving in and out, not about the firn changing volume.
Nothing is sealed in the upper firn yet. Paragraph 4 places trapping below the lock in zone.
The passage never mentions anything living in the firn. The image is entirely about air moving in and out.
The passage describes firn gaining mass and compacting under new snow, not wasting away.

questions.stem: As used in paragraph 16, "floor" most nearly means
choices: an upper bound on how fast past change could have been
a lower bound on how fast change could have been
the lowest temperature ever reached in the polar regions
the base of the ice sheet where it rests on bedrock
the deepest section of a core that can still be counted

proof.quote: sets a floor under past rates of change rather than a ceiling
both hide fast changes and preserve slow ones

questions.why: Paragraph 16 says smoothing and thinning hide fast change, so the record can show that change was at least this fast without ruling out something faster. A floor is the lower bound, and the paragraph sets it against a ceiling.
distractorNotes: That is the ceiling the paragraph says the record does not give, and a floor works the other way.
Here the word limits a rate of change, not a temperature.
This is the literal sense of the word, but the paragraph is discussing limits on a rate, not the bottom of an ice sheet.
Depth comes up nearby, though the phrase is about how fast past change could have been, not about where counting stops.

questions.stem: It can be inferred from paragraph 5 that a conclusion about whether carbon dioxide rose before or after a warming is most trustworthy when it is drawn from
choices: the deepest ice available at a site, since it covers by far the longest span of time
a single core, so that only one chronology is involved
gas measurements alone, with the ice measurements set aside entirely
an interior site where the firn column is unusually deep and cold
a site where the ice age and the gas age are close together

proof.quote: the two sit on different clocks
The uncertainty in that correction is often larger than the lead or the lag under debate.
from a few decades at a wet coastal site to several thousand years

questions.why: Paragraph 5 says the correction for the age offset is often larger than the lead or lag being argued about, so the smaller that offset is, the less the answer depends on the model.
distractorNotes: Length of record does not help with sequencing, and paragraph 14 adds that the deepest ice is the least trustworthy of all.
Using one core does not shrink the offset between the two clocks inside that same core.
The comparison needs both, since the temperature signal is read from the ice and the gas is read from the bubbles.
A deeper firn column takes longer to seal air, which makes the offset larger and the correction harder.

questions.stem: Paragraph 10 suggests that a temperature history built from water isotopes could be misleading if
choices: the core was drilled at a site with unusually heavy snowfall
the laboratory measured deuterium instead of oxygen-18
the surrounding ice contained unusually large amounts of volcanic sulfate
the height of the ice sheet surface changed over the period covered
the bubbles in the core closed off at a shallower depth than usual

proof.quote: If the ice sheet stood taller, its surface was colder for reasons unrelated to the climate at sea level.
that the ice surface stood at the same elevation

questions.why: Paragraph 10 lists constant surface elevation as one of the assumptions behind the reading, then notes that a taller ice sheet had a colder surface for reasons unrelated to the climate at sea level.
distractorNotes: Heavy snowfall helps the record by improving resolution. The worry in this paragraph is season, moisture source, and elevation.
The passage treats deuterium and oxygen-18 as two versions of the same signal, not as a source of error.
Sulfate is a dating marker in paragraph 13 and is never said to distort the isotope thermometer.
Close off depth changes the age of the gas, which is paragraph 4, not the isotope ratio measured in the ice itself.

questions.stem: Which of the following best states the central point of the passage?
choices: Ice cores have proven beyond argument that carbon dioxide and temperature have always risen and fallen together
The water isotope thermometer should be abandoned in favor of borehole and trapped gas methods
Ice holds a usable record of past air, but each step from snowfall to number adds a limit to account for
Deep drilling in Antarctica has extended the climate record much further back than drilling in Greenland
Layer counting is the only dependable way to assign an age to anything found inside an ice core

proof.quote: What it holds is an archive.
That last clause carries the first complication
The thermometer is not wrong, but it is conditional
An archive whose distortions are known and bounded is worth far more than one that merely looks clean.

questions.why: The passage traces snow into ice, then into a readable record, and at every stage names what is lost or shifted. Paragraph 17 states the point outright: the archive is valuable because its distortions are known and bounded.
distractorNotes: The passage says the ordering of the two is exactly what the age offset makes hard to establish.
Paragraph 11 presents those methods as checks that correct the isotope reading, not as replacements for it.
The length of the Antarctic record is one detail in paragraph 15, not the argument the whole passage builds.
Paragraphs 13 and 15 add volcanic horizons, solar events and flow models as further ways of assigning ages.

questions.stem: The main function of paragraph 11 in the passage is to
choices: introduce a second and more reliable method for dating the layers in a core
show that the record carries its own checks on the isotope reading
argue that measurements made on the ice are more reliable than measurements made on the gas
explain why the deepest sections of a core cannot be counted year by year
describe how heat from the interior of the Earth reaches the base of an ice sheet

proof.quote: What rescues it is that the ice offers thermometers of other kinds.
close to twice what the spatial slope alone suggested

questions.why: Paragraph 10 ends by calling the isotope thermometer conditional. Paragraph 11 opens with what rescues it and gives two other thermometers, one of which revised the Greenland estimate by about a factor of two.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 11 is about temperature, not age. Dating begins in the paragraph that follows it.
One of the two checks it describes, the isotope sorting of nitrogen and argon, is a measurement made on the trapped gas.
That problem belongs to paragraph 14, which takes up the difficulties of the deepest ice.
Geothermal heat appears in paragraph 14 as a way the oldest ice is lost, not as the subject of this paragraph.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes how the passage is organized?
choices: It traces snow into ice, then how the record is read and dated, and finally what it can claim
It compares the Greenland and Antarctic drilling programs and judges which of them is better
It states a conclusion about past climate and then works backward through the evidence supporting it
It moves through the seasons of a single year of snowfall and then repeats the cycle at greater depth
It alternates between describing a measurement and describing an eruption that confirms it

proof.quote: Turning snow into ice is slow mechanical work.
The chain of reasoning turns a chemical ratio into a thermometer.
Dating begins with counting.
All of this shapes what the record can say about rates.

questions.why: The passage runs in order: snow to firn to sealed bubbles in paragraphs 2 through 6, then the isotope thermometer and the dating methods, then the deepest ice, and finally what the record can and cannot say about rates.
distractorNotes: Both regions appear, but as sources of different kinds of information, and they are never ranked against each other.
No conclusion is stated up front. The passage builds its cautions as it goes and gathers them at the end.
Seasonal layering appears only as a dating method in paragraph 12, not as the plan of the passage.
Volcanic eruptions appear once, as a way of pinning a layer count, not as a recurring pattern.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the water isotope thermometer in paragraph 10 is best described as
choices: dismissive of a method that rests on assumptions that no one is able to test
enthusiastic about a technique that requires no further checking
indifferent to whether the method gives an accurate temperature
puzzled by a result that nobody working in the field has managed to explain
accepting of the method while insisting that its assumptions be stated

proof.quote: The thermometer is not wrong, but it is conditional
it is worth being blunt about what the reading assumes

questions.why: Paragraph 10 lists what the reading assumes, says none of it holds exactly, and then says plainly that the thermometer is not wrong but conditional. That is acceptance with conditions attached.
distractorNotes: The paragraph says the thermometer is not wrong, and the next paragraph shows the assumptions being tested.
The paragraph spends most of its length on what the reading takes for granted, which is not enthusiasm.
Accuracy is the entire concern of the paragraph, and the author cares enough to list what can bias it.
Nothing here is left unexplained. The author explains each assumption and how it can skew the result.

questions.stem: In paragraph 16, the author treats the claim that no past rise matched the speed of the present one as
choices: an overstatement the ice record cannot support at all
a conclusion that the deepest Antarctic cores establish most firmly
a question that further deep drilling will have to settle one way or another
sound, but only because well resolved records stand behind it
less interesting than the question of how the layers are counted

proof.quote: That claim holds up because it does not rest on the deep cores.
resolve the last two thousand years to a decade or better

questions.why: Paragraph 16 says the claim is only as strong as the resolution of the ice behind it, then says it holds up because it rests on heavy snowfall sites that resolve the last two thousand years to a decade or better.
distractorNotes: The author says the claim holds up, and names the evidence that carries it.
The paragraph says the claim survives precisely because it does not rest on the deep cores.
The author treats the question as already answered by the well resolved recent record.
Counting is discussed earlier as a tool. Here the author is judging the rate claim itself, not ranking the two topics.

questions.stem: The passage names all of the following as reasons the deepest ice is hard to trust EXCEPT
choices: layers are thinned by the spreading of the ice sheet until single years are very thin
the bubbles at that depth have leaked their gas into the nearby ice
diffusion of water molecules through solid ice erases the annual isotope cycles
heat from below can melt away the oldest ice at the base
flow around obstacles near bedrock can place older ice above younger ice

proof.quote: every annual layer is stretched sideways and thinned as it is buried
diffusion of water molecules through the solid smears the isotope cycles
Geothermal heat can melt the bottom away
stacking older ice above younger

questions.why: Paragraph 14 lists thinning, isotope diffusion, basal melting and folding near bedrock. Leaking bubbles are never mentioned anywhere in the passage.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 14 describes exactly this thinning, from twenty centimeters at the surface to a fraction of a millimeter near the bed.
Paragraph 14 names this smearing as one reason annual structure disappears at depth.
Paragraph 14 says geothermal heat can melt the bottom away and remove the oldest ice.
Paragraph 14 describes ice folding back over itself near bedrock and stacking older ice above younger.

questions.stem: A reader looking for an explanation of how a volcanic eruption helps fix the age of a layer would find it in
choices: paragraph 3, on how deep the open firn column runs
paragraph 7, on what the ice carries besides trapped air
paragraph 10, on the assumptions that sit behind the isotope thermometer
paragraph 13, on the tie points that keep a layer count from drifting
paragraph 14, on the problems that affect the deepest ice

proof.quote: Eruptions with known historical dates anchor the recent count outright.
leaving one horizon that shows up in Greenland and Antarctic cores alike

questions.why: Paragraph 13 explains that a large eruption lays down one sulfate horizon in both hemispheres, and that eruptions with known historical dates anchor the recent count.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 3 is about how far the firn exchanges air with the atmosphere, not about dating.
Paragraph 7 mentions sulfate as a marker of eruptions but does not explain how it pins a chronology.
Paragraph 10 is about reconstructing temperature, not about assigning ages to layers.
Paragraph 14 explains why deep layers are unreliable, not how eruptions anchor a count.
